53: In 1880 the British sent Kinthup, a Lepcha from Sikkim, to float 500 marked logs down Tibet's Tsangpo to prove it becomes the Brahmaputra. Sold into slavery twice, he finally launched them, but his letter had gone unread and nobody watched for them downstream. His findings were only vindicated in 1913.
136: Dimapur, Nagaland's largest city, takes its name from this river, called Dima (big water) in the Dimasa language; "pur" means settlement. It was the medieval Kachari capital until the Ahoms sacked it in the 16th century, and its mushroom-domed stone pillars still stand.
380: Acid draining from rat-hole coal mines in Meghalaya has made its water corrosive enough to eat into the Kopili hydro project near Umrangso. In October 2019 a weakened penstock burst there, killing four workers and destroying most of the machinery.
859: The 2,000 MW Subansiri Lower project at Gerukamukh, on the Assam-Arunachal border, is India's largest hydropower project. Approved in 2003, it stalled for most of 2011-2019 amid downstream protests and safety reviews, and its first units began commercial operation only in late 2025.
863: Until a great flood in 1787, the Teesta flowed south towards the Ganga through channels such as the Atrai and Karatoya; the flood turned it southeast into the Brahmaputra. In October 2023 a glacial lake outburst flood destroyed the Teesta III dam at Chungthang in Sikkim within minutes.
864: In late 2017 the Siang turned black, sparking rumours that Chinese dams or tunnels upstream were to blame. Satellite images showed the real cause: earthquakes up to magnitude 6.4 near Gyala Peri in Tibet set off about 100 sq km of landslides, pushing turbidity to 425 NTU against a normal 12-15.
872: It starts in Tibet's Chumbi Valley as the Machu, becomes the Amo Chu in Bhutan, flows past the border towns of Phuentsholing and Jaigaon, and then runs by Jaldapara National Park, home to India's largest one-horned rhino population after Kaziranga.
902: The 2,880 MW Dibang Multipurpose Project, launched in 2024, will be India's tallest dam at 278 metres and is billed as the world's tallest roller-compacted-concrete dam. Its foundation stone had first been laid back in 2008; completion is targeted for 2032.
950: Manas National Park, where the river forms the India-Bhutan border, lost all its rhinos to poaching during the Bodo insurgency and was put on UNESCO's World Heritage in Danger list in 1992. Rhinos were reintroduced from 2007, and the park came off the danger list in 2011.
959: The 9.15 km Bhupen Hazarika Setu between Dhola and Sadiya, opened in 2017, spans this river and was built to carry 60-tonne battle tanks, giving the Army a fast road towards the China border in eastern Arunachal.
1050: Loktak Lake drains into this river, and the Ithai Barrage on it (operational 1983) keeps the lake at a near-constant level for hydropower. That stopped the floating phumdis from sinking each dry season to take up nutrients, thinning the floating Keibul Lamjao park, last home of the sangai deer.
1844: India's oldest known human fossil, a skull found by geologist Arun Sonakia in 1982 on the Narmada's north bank near Hoshangabad (Narmadapuram), is known as Narmada Man. The valley also lent its name to a dinosaur: Rajasaurus narmadensis, a large predator that lived here about 67 million years ago.
2071: In 1996, tribal villagers displaced by the Tawa dam formed the Tawa Matsya Sangh, a cooperative that won the right to fish the reservoir that had flooded their land. Under it the yearly catch rose from 93 tonnes in its first season to 393 tonnes by 1999-2000.
2293: The Sabarmati Riverfront in Ahmedabad, a mixed-use waterfront on banks once lined with slums, is one of India's earliest large river-bank rejuvenation projects; around 5,000 families were relocated to build it. The river itself carries little water at Ahmedabad for much of the year: since 2002 the city stretch has been topped up with Narmada canal water, held back by the Vasna Barrage.
2569: Alandi on its banks holds the samadhi of Sant Dnyaneshwar, who entombed himself there in 1296 aged 21; pilgrims bathe in the river before darshan. Maharashtra's scented Indrayani rice is also named after it: bred at the Rice Research Station at Vadgaon Maval, in the Maval country the river drains, and released in 1987, it now covers the largest paddy area in western Maharashtra.
2694: The Koyna flows east to the Krishna, but the water held in its Shivasagar reservoir is sent west through tunnels to power stations hidden deep inside the Western Ghats, then on to the Arabian Sea near Chiplun. For the project's fourth stage, engineers blasted an intake through the lake bed, reportedly the first of its kind in Asia.
2744: The UNESCO World Heritage temples of Pattadakal stand on the Malaprabha's west bank, where the river turns to flow north, a direction Hindu tradition considers auspicious. The name means 'stone of coronation': Chalukya kings such as Vinayaditya were crowned there in the 7th century. Aihole, another Chalukyan temple town, is about 10 km away.
2776: On 12 July 1961, after weeks of record rain, the new Panshet dam upstream burst at about 3:30 am in its very first year of storing water. Its flood overwhelmed the Khadakwasla dam on the Mutha, which gave way at 7:30 am and sent a wall of water through Pune, the worst disaster in the city's history.
2821: Its name means 'five rivers': the Kasari, Kumbhi, Tulsi and Bhogavati, plus a Saraswati that local tradition says joins underground. Their meeting point near Kolhapur is revered as a Prayag, like Allahabad's. Kolhapur tracks monsoon floods by the river's level at the Rajaram weir, where the danger mark is 43 feet.
2827: At Chinchwad, the samadhi temple of Morya Gosavi stands on its bank. He was the Ganapatya saint whose name is popularly taken to be the 'Morya' in 'Ganpati Bappa Morya'. Locals treat the riverside temple going under water as a sign of really heavy rain in Pimpri-Chinchwad.
2911: A Kannada saying, 'Tunga paana, Ganga snana', advises: drink the Tunga's sweet water, bathe in the holy Ganga. The Sringeri Sharada Peetham, the matha associated with Adi Shankara, stands on its banks. At Koodli near Shivamogga the Tunga joins the Bhadra to form the Tungabhadra.
2912: The Tungabhadra Dam near Hosapete, commissioned in 1953, was built with traditional surki (lime and mud) mortar instead of cement. It is India's largest stone masonry dam and one of only two non-cement dams in the country, the other being Mullaperiyar in Kerala. In August 2024 a crest gate was swept away, its first such damage in 70 years.
2932: Under the Treaty of Warna, concluded at Varna on 26 April 1731, Chhatrapati Shahu of Satara and his cousin Sambhaji II of Kolhapur ended their war of succession for the Maratha throne. Sambhaji gave up all claims north of the river, which became the border: Satara to the north, Kolhapur to the south. Kolhapur lasted as a princely state until it merged into Bombay State in 1949.
2961: At Pandharpur it is called the Chandrabhaga, said to be because it curves like a crescent moon there. Varkari pilgrims bathe in it before going for darshan at the Vithoba temple, above all on Ashadhi and Kartiki Ekadashi, when the Ashadhi yatra alone draws around a million people.
3014: At Gokak Falls the Ghataprabha drops 52 m over a horseshoe-shaped sandstone cliff. A hydroelectric station set up there in 1887 to power the neighbouring Gokak cotton mill was one of India's earliest. The mill still spins yarn today.
3217: Peshwa Madhavrao I, ill with tuberculosis, spent his last days at the Chintamani temple at Theur, which the river surrounds on three sides. He died there in November 1772, aged 27, and his wife Ramabai committed sati on his funeral pyre. A stone memorial marks the spot.
3218: The legendary Golconda diamonds, including the Hope Diamond and, it is believed, the Koh-i-Noor, were dug from gravel pits along the banks of the lower Krishna, such as the Kollur mine on its south bank. Geologists think the stones were washed there from ancient kimberlite rocks upstream.
3220: On 28-29 September 1908 the Musi flooded Hyderabad, killing an estimated 15,000 or more people. The Nizam called in M. Visvesvaraya, and the twin reservoirs Osman Sagar (opened 1921) and Himayat Sagar (1927) were built upstream to protect the city. Both also supplied the city's drinking water.
3268: Known as the 'Sorrow of Vijayawada', this rivulet drains into Kolleru Lake, not the Krishna. A diversion channel sends its floodwater to the Krishna above Prakasam Barrage. In September 2024 the flow far exceeded what the channel could carry, and breaches in the Budameru's banks flooded large parts of the city.
3339: The Borra Caves, a limestone cave system in the Ananthagiri hills of the Araku Valley, were carved by the Gosthani. They lie about 705 m above sea level, reach 80 m below ground, and were explored by the British geologist William King George in 1807.
3498: The beach at its mouth in Ganjam is one of the world's great olive ridley turtle rookeries. In February 2025 nearly 7 lakh turtles came ashore to nest in about a week, the biggest mass nesting (arribada) recorded there, beating 6.37 lakh in 2023.
3669: The Madras Boat Club has rowed on the Adyar since 1892, and its Madras-Colombo Regatta, held since 1898, is thought to be among the world's oldest inter-club regattas. The river also named the Adyar neighbourhood, and through it the Adyar Ananda Bhavan (A2B) chain: K.S. Thirupathi Raja's restaurant was simply Ananda Bhavan until a branch opened in Adyar in 1988.
3723: Fort St George was built on a sandbank between the sea, the Cooum to the south and a second river to the west, the Elambore or North River, which joined the Cooum at its mouth. A cut joining the two rivers turned the marsh between them into today's Island Grounds. The Elambore was diverted westwards in the 1750s to enlarge the fort, and the Buckingham Canal now follows its old course.
4073: Sangam poems such as the Paripatal celebrate the Vaigai. Since 2015, digs at Keezhadi on its banks, about 12 km south-east of Madurai, have uncovered an ancient urban settlement with brick buildings, ring wells, terracotta pipes and pottery inscribed in Tamil-Brahmi script.
4118: At Adichanallur near Tirunelveli, on the banks of the Thamirabarani, German researcher Dr. Jagor dug up pottery and iron implements in 1876. Later excavations found over 160 urns holding skeletons, dated to about 900-700 BCE, and an on-site museum is being built at the spot.
4946: The Godavari delta became Andhra's 'rice bowl' after British engineer Sir Arthur Cotton built the Dowleswaram anicut near Rajahmundry between 1847 and 1852. He is still so revered that during the 2015 Godavari Pushkaram people performed traditional ancestral rites in his honour, and a museum in Rajamahendravaram is named after him.
5060: At Sutapadar on the Odisha-Chhattisgarh border, the river splits in two. One arm, the Jora Nala, slips away into the Sabari (Kolab). As more water took that route, summer flows towards Jagdalpur and Chitrakote shrank, so the two states now regulate the split with a control structure at the mouth of the Jora Nala.
5395: This stream so captivated Viswanatha Satyanarayana, later the first Telugu writer to win the Jnanpith Award, that he wrote 'Kinnerasani Patalu' (Songs of Kinnerasani), one of his best-loved lyrical works. Today the dam near Paloncha is ringed by the Kinnerasani Wildlife Sanctuary.
5657: The Manjira Wildlife Sanctuary, a reservoir stretch about 50 km from Hyderabad that also supplies the city's water, began as a refuge for mugger crocodiles. From just four pairs in 1974, the population has grown to an estimated 400 to 600. Downstream, the Nizam Sagar dam (1923-31) is Telangana's oldest dam and submerged over 40 villages.
6072: Formed where the Wardha meets the Wainganga, the Pranhita runs only about 113 km, yet its system drains roughly a third of the Godavari basin. Every 12 years, when Jupiter enters Pisces, pilgrims gather for the Pranahita Pushkaralu, most of all at Kaleshwaram where it joins the Godavari. The last one was in April 2022.
6541: In Kipling's The Jungle Book, Shere Khan is 'the tiger who lived near the Waingunga River', and Mowgli's jungle is set in the Seoni hills where the river rises. Kipling never went there: he wrote the stories at his desk in Vermont, relying on books such as R. A. Sterndale's account of life in Seoni.
6829: Untreated waste from tanneries around Vellore poisoned the Palar and the farmland it waters. The resulting case, Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996), is a landmark: the Supreme Court used it to formally adopt the 'polluter pays' and 'precautionary' principles into Indian environmental law.
6873: Just before the Amaravathi dam (1957), inside the Anamalai hills' Indira Gandhi Wildlife Sanctuary, lies the Amaravathi Sagar Crocodile Farm. Set up in 1976, it is described as India's largest crocodile nursery and breeds mugger crocodiles for release.
6957: The Bhavanisagar Dam, completed in 1955, is described as one of the largest earthen dams in the world. Where the river meets the Kaveri, the town of Bhavani gives its name to the Bhavani Jamakkalam, handwoven cotton carpets that received a GI tag in 2005-06.
6983: In 1902 a power station at Shivanasamudra Falls on the Kaveri, one of the earliest hydroelectric plants in Asia, began sending electricity to the mines of the Kolar Gold Fields. Its power was later extended to light up Bengaluru and Mysuru.
7112: Near Hassan, the Gothic Holy Rosary Church at Shettihalli, built by French missionaries around 1860, was swallowed by the Hemavathi reservoir at Gorur. It goes under during the monsoon (July to October) and re-emerges as a ruin from about December to May.
7443: Effluent from Tiruppur's textile dyeing units polluted the Noyyal so badly that the Orathupalayam dam on it was decommissioned and now just stores effluent. In January 2011, on a case brought by farmers, the Madras High Court ordered over 700 bleaching and dyeing units shut until they achieved zero liquid discharge.
7714: The Kollidam branches off the Kaveri at Mukkombu, about 18 km west of Tiruchirappalli, where Sir Arthur Cotton built the Upper Anicut in 1836-38. The two channels enclose the temple island of Srirangam. Near the sea, the Pichavaram mangroves, one of India's largest, lie between its estuary and the Vellar's.
7730: Before Kaveri water was piped in, Bengaluru drank from the Arkavathy. Dewan Seshadri Iyer began the Chamarajendra waterworks at Hesaraghatta in 1891, meant to serve 250,000 people. When it ran dry by 1918, the Thippagondanahalli reservoir followed in 1933, on the advice of a Visvesvaraya committee.
8440: In August 2006, huge emergency releases from the Ukai Dam during a monsoon surge sent the Tapi through Surat, flooding about 80 to 95% of the city. Upstream, the river's source town of Multai in the Satpuras takes its name from 'Multapi', the origin of the Tapi.
8641: Chapora Fort, high above the river's mouth, became one of Goa's top attractions after it featured in the 2001 film Dil Chahta Hai. Originally the Adil Shahi 'Shahpoora', it changed hands between the Portuguese and Marathas, and the Portuguese added escape tunnels to the riverbank in 1717.
8654: It starts at Tulsi Lake inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park and was once pretty enough for Hindi film shoots. The 1957 Dilip Kumar and Vyjayanthimala film Naya Daur is said to have been shot beside it, and crocodiles reportedly lived in it until the late 1960s.

Dahisar railway station is named after Dahisar village, not the river: the village name is traced to Dadhicheshwar, a temple of the sage Dadhichi mentioned in the medieval Mahikavatichi Bakhar. Elsewhere stations take a river's name, like Vaitarna on the same Western line, or Krishna in Telangana, whose platform begins at the river's edge.
8744: The Kaiga nuclear power station stands near the Kali, inland from Karwar. In December 2018 one of its units set a world record of 962 days of continuous operation among all nuclear power plants. Upstream, the river's rapids near Dandeli are a popular white-water rafting spot from October to March.
8808: Goa's floating casinos are ships anchored in the Mandovi off Panaji. Goa's gambling law allows casinos only in five-star hotels and on offshore vessels, so guests are ferried out to them on small feeder boats.
8809: Vihar Lake (finished in 1860) and Powai Lake (1891) are British-era reservoirs built on the Mithi and one of its streams to supply Bombay with water. Powai's water was soon judged unfit to drink. Downstream, the river passes through a culvert beneath the runway of Mumbai's airport.
8856: It serves as the tailrace of Tata Power's Khopoli hydro station, which began generating in 1915 and is one of India's earliest. Monsoon water stored in lakes up on the Ghats near Lonavala drops through its turbines into the river, keeping it flowing all year for towns and factories from Khopoli down to Rasayani and Panvel.
8917: Tansa Dam, finished in 1892 about 110 km north of Bombay, sent water to the city purely by gravity, through a 42 km masonry aqueduct along the hill ridges and pipelines across the valleys. A steel bridge built in 1925 to carry Tansa pipes over Thane Creek near Kasheli later became part of the Mumbai-Agra highway.
8922: Tiracol village, on the river's north bank at its mouth, belongs to Goa but is cut off from the rest of the state by the river and is reached mainly by ferry from Querim. On 15 August 1954, satyagrahis protesting Portuguese rule occupied Fort Tiracol and flew the Indian flag for a day before being arrested.
8949: Mugger crocodiles live in the Vashishti around Chiplun. Locals run two-hour 'crocodile safari' boat rides at low tide to spot them, including near Maldoli, and residents put the local population at around 20, though no official count has been done.
8958: In four villages along the Zuari near Ponda, farmers still perform Maange Thapnee. They mould a crocodile out of field mud, decorate it with vermilion and flowers and make offerings, honouring the estuary's mugger crocodiles as protectors of their paddy fields. The ritual is usually held around the January new moon.
8960: White-water rafting at Kolad goes on well beyond the monsoon. Almost every morning, water released from the Bhira dam upstream turns the gentle Kundalika into a run of grade II-III rapids, and rafting trips are timed to the release.
8965: The SS Vaitarna, a steamship named after this river, vanished in a cyclone off Saurashtra on 8 November 1888 with 746 people aboard. Locals called it Vijli (electricity) for its electric lights, and Gujarati folklore remembers it as the 'Titanic of Gujarat', 24 years before the Titanic sank.
8969: On 27 July 2019 the swollen Ulhas flooded the railway tracks between Badlapur and Vangani and stranded the Kolhapur-bound Mahalaxmi Express in deep water for 12 to 15 hours. The NDRF, Navy, Air Force, police and Vangani villagers rescued all of its passengers, several hundred of them, including nine pregnant women.
8975: It is one of five rivers said to rise at the Panchganga temple in Old Mahabaleshwar, built in the 13th century by the Seuna king Simhana. Its sisters, the Krishna, Koyna and Venna, end up in the Bay of Bengal, but the Savitri drops west down the Ghats past Mahad to the Arabian Sea near Harihareshwar.
9009: Our Lady of Remedy Church in Poisar village, Kandivali West, dates from the Portuguese era of the 1550s (accounts give 1550 or 1555), making it one of Mumbai's oldest churches still in use. It is a Grade II-A listed heritage structure.
9155: Every 12 years until 1755, Thirunavaya on the banks of the Nila hosted the Mamankam, a great fair presided over by the Zamorin of Kozhikode. Warriors from leading Nair families of rival Valluvanad came on suicide missions to try to kill him.
9161: Athirappilly Falls on the Chalakudy, nicknamed the 'Niagara of South India', has appeared in films from 'Dil Se' (1998) to 'Baahubali: The Beginning' (2015). The 1986 Tamil hit 'Punnagai Mannan' made it so popular that Tamil audiences called it 'Punnagai Mannan Falls'.
9162: At Beypore, where the Chaliyar meets the sea, craftsmen still build the 'uru', a large wooden dhow of Arab origin that is exported to the Middle East. Kerala's first railway line, opened in 1861, ran from Tirur to Beypore on this estuary.
9293: Punalur's suspension bridge over the Kallada, built in 1877 under the Travancore government, is called South India's first motorable bridge. It was designed to sway so that wild animals from the forest would not cross into town. Local lore says its engineer rowed under it with his family while six elephants walked across, to prove it was safe.
9525: At Uppinangady the Netravati and Kumaradhara flow past either side of the Sahasralingeshwara temple. In very heavy monsoon floods they rise until they meet at the temple's entrance. Devotees wait for this 'Sangama', then hold a Sangama Pooja and bathe in the merged waters, as in August 2018.
9550: Every February since 1895, the Maramon Convention, described as Asia's largest Christian convention, has been held on the Pamba's vast sandbed near Kozhencherry. Downriver at Aranmula, snake boats race on the same river during Onam in the Uthrattathi boat race, the oldest river boat festival in Kerala.
9687: The Muthappan temple at Parassinikadavu, on the banks of the Valapattanam near Kannur, stages Theyyam every morning and evening. Unusually for a Hindu temple, its customary offerings are fish, meat and toddy. Dogs are revered there, since Muthappan is said to have always travelled with one.
9726: At Jog Falls the Sharavati drops about 253 m in four streams nicknamed Raja, Rani, Roarer and Rocket. Their flow is now controlled by the upstream Linganamakki dam, which feeds the Mahatma Gandhi hydroelectric station (running since 1948), so the falls are fullest when the dam releases water.
9727: The Mullaperiyar dam, opened in 1895 under Colonel John Pennycuick, sends part of this west-flowing Kerala river eastwards through a tunnel into Tamil Nadu's Vaigai basin to irrigate farmland. Pennycuick is still honoured there: his statue stands at the PWD office in Madurai.
10137: Dhauli hill on its bank, just south of Bhubaneswar, is widely believed to be the Kalinga War battlefield that turned Ashoka towards Buddhism. His rock edicts are carved there, and the Peace Pagoda on the hilltop was built by Japanese and Odia Buddhist groups in 1972. The river ends in Chilika Lake.
10943: In 1998 a 23 km stretch near Durg was handed to a private company, Radius Water, for a token lease of Re 1 a year, to supply industries at the Borai industrial estate. It was India's first experiment in privatising a river. Villagers lost access for fishing and irrigation, and a legislative committee later recommended cancelling the deal.
11076: When the Hirakud reservoir filled in the 1950s, it drowned more than 200 temples. About 50 of them still surface in peak summer when the water drops, and in 2014 inscribed stones believed to be from the Padmaseni temple of the submerged town of Padampur were recovered.
11080: Its Hasdeo Bango dam, Chhattisgarh's first multipurpose water project, is officially named after Minimata. A Satnami leader and one of the region's first women MPs, she campaigned against untouchability, child marriage and dowry.
11466: Its name means "streak of gold": gold was once mined near its source at Piska near Ranchi, and people still sift its sands for tiny gold particles. Ritwik Ghatak named his 1965 Partition film Subarnarekha after the river.
11787: This is where Alexander the Great's march into India ended. In 326 BCE his exhausted army mutinied on the banks of the Beas, which the Greeks called the Hyphasis, and refused to go further east. Alexander raised twelve giant altars there to mark the limit of his conquests, then turned back.
12067: The Chenab Rail Bridge near Reasi, opened on 6 June 2025, carries trains 359 m above the riverbed, making it the world's highest railway bridge, about 35 m taller than the Eiffel Tower. It is a key link of the line that finally connected the Kashmir Valley to India's rail network.
12552: It is named after Ghulam Rasool Galwan (1878-1925), a Ladakhi caravan leader who guided European explorers. His memoir, 'Servant of Sahibs', written in English he had picked up on his travels, was published in Cambridge in 1923 with an introduction by Francis Younghusband.
12783: Hanle village, which it flows past, hosts the Indian Astronomical Observatory at about 4,500 m, among the highest in the world. In 2022 the surrounding area became India's first dark-sky reserve.
12954: The Jhelum's main source is the Verinag spring in south Kashmir, where Emperor Jahangir built an octagonal stone tank around the spring in 1620; Shah Jahan later added a garden. Jahangir loved the spot so much he wished to be buried there, but the wish was not carried out and his tomb is in Lahore.
14119: It is born from meltwater streams pouring out of ice caves at the snout of the Siachen Glacier. Lower down, the Nubra valley's sand dunes at Hunder host double-humped Bactrian camels, descendants of animals left behind when the Silk Route trade to Yarkand ended around 1950.
14248: At Manikaran, on its right bank, springs at 64-80°C are hot enough to cook in: the langar of Gurdwara Manikaran Sahib cooks food in large vessels set in the spring water, and visitors boil rice tied in cloth bags.
14982: Tabo Monastery on its bank was founded in 996 CE by the translator Rinchen Zangpo and is considered the oldest continuously functioning Buddhist monastery in India and the Himalaya. Its murals and frescoes have earned it the nickname 'Ajanta of the Himalayas'.
15362: Water stored at Barot drops through a mountain to the Shanan Power House at Jogindernagar, commissioned in 1932, which lit up undivided Punjab, Lahore and Delhi before Independence. Built on a 99-year lease from the Raja of Mandi and still run by Punjab, its ownership has been before the Supreme Court since the lease ran out in 2024.
15426: This is the Kali Bein of Sultanpur Lodhi, where Guru Nanak is said to have attained enlightenment. From 2000, environmentalist Sant Balbir Singh Seechewal led a volunteer kar sewa, about 3,000 people a day for three and a half years, to revive the choked, polluted stream.
15534: Its name is often explained as Yarkandi for 'river of death'. In August 1929 the Chong Kumdan glacier, which had surged across its upper valley, released the lake dammed behind it; the flood raised the Indus at Attock, about 1,200 km downstream, by nearly 27 feet.
15535: The Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Ghaghara all rise within about 60 km of one another near Mount Kailash in Tibet. From that one corner of the plateau the Indus heads west to the Arabian Sea, while the Brahmaputra loops east and ends up in the Bay of Bengal.
15541: On 31 December 1929 Jawaharlal Nehru hoisted the tricolour on the banks of the Ravi at Lahore after the Congress resolved to seek Purna Swaraj, complete independence. Congress then asked Indians to observe 26 January 1930 as Independence Day, which is why 26 January was later chosen as Republic Day.
15544: Jammu Tawi (code JAT), the city's main railway station, is a rare Indian station named after both its city and its river. It opened in 1972; Jammu's first railway, an 1890 line to Sialkot, was cut at Partition, leaving the city without trains for over two decades.
15546: In deep winter its gorge freezes into a thick sheet of ice called the 'chadar'. For generations, with the only road over Pensi La snowed shut, walking this frozen river down to Nimmu was the Zanskaris' winter lifeline; it is now the famous Chadar trek, and a new road is being cut along the gorge.
15848: The Sutlej is older than the Himalaya. It is an antecedent river: as the mountains rose it kept cutting down through them, which is why it slices right across the range from Tibet and enters India at the Shipki La pass in Himachal Pradesh.
15857: It never reaches the sea, petering out in the Thar desert. On its now-dry lower course in Rajasthan lies Kalibangan, a Harappan site where archaeologists uncovered a ploughed field from about 2800 BCE, the earliest ever found by excavation, and signs of an earthquake around 2600 BCE.
15985: Looping from Madhya Pradesh through Rajasthan into Gujarat, the Mahi crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice. The silt it carries helped make the Gulf of Khambhat shallow, contributing to the decline of the gulf's once-prosperous ports.
16068: It runs through the middle of Vadodara, a city of about 3 million, and is home to at least 300 mugger crocodiles. When it floods, the crocodiles wander into the city: 22 were rescued from residential areas within a week of the 2019 floods.
16127: At Jetpur, a big centre for sari dyeing and printing, dye waste once turned the Bhadar and nearby wells and ponds crimson. In August 1997 the Gujarat High Court ordered about 1,200 dyeing and printing units shut and fined the industry Rs 1.25 crore. They reopened a month later on condition of building treatment plants.
16499: Asiatic lions that have spread out of Gir now use the Shetrunji's banks as a corridor, and some live near its dam at Palitana. Pilgrims on the steps of the Jain holy hill of Shatrunjaya filmed a lion there in October 2025, and three were seen there in 2020.
16577: Its Sanskrit name, Lavanavari, means 'salt river'. The water is fresh in its upper course but turns saline from around Balotra as it crosses the desert, and the river never reaches the sea, petering out in the marshes of the Rann of Kutch.
16609: Tradition treats this river as the sacred Sarasvati: Siddhpur on its banks is revered as Matru Gaya, held to be the only place in India for a mother's shraddha rites. But a 2017 study that drilled the Rann of Kutch for the lost Vedic Sarasvati, which some scholars trace through the Ghaggar-Hakra towards the Rann, found this Aravalli stream has "no connection with the Vedic counterpart".
16669: Banaskantha ('bank of the Banas') district is named after this river, and the district in turn gave its name to Banas Dairy in Palanpur, described as Asia's largest milk cooperative, which collects over 8 million litres a day. The river itself never reaches the sea; it ends in the Little Rann of Kutch.
17152: Known as the Tlawng in Mizoram, it is Aizawl's main water source, but it flows more than 1,000 metres below the city. Its water is pumped up in seven stages to a hilltop reservoir at about 1,030 metres, which makes the supply very costly to run.
17334: The Dumbur dam, commissioned in 1976, created a lake of about 41 sq km, Tripura's largest water body. It drowned the fertile Raima-Sarma valley, once called Tripura's granary, displacing thousands of families, many of whom became fishers on the new lake.
19054: In winter its water at Dawki is so clear that boats seem to float in mid-air. The single-lane suspension bridge across it there, on the road to the Tamabil crossing into Bangladesh, was built by the British in 1932.
19186: Born in the Manipur hills, where the Poumai Nagas call it the Vourei, the Barak splits in two on the Assam-Bangladesh border into the Surma and the Kushiyara. The two branches reunite inside Bangladesh as the Meghna, one of the three great rivers that build the Ganga delta.
19722: It rises at Gonasika in the hills near Keonjhar, emerging from a rock shaped like a cow's nostril (go-nasika), then disappears underground for about half a kilometre before resurfacing. It shares its name with the mythical Vaitarani that souls must cross to reach Yama.
20458: It is born at Vedvyas on the edge of Rourkela, where the South Koel and Sankh meet. Local legend says sage Parashara met the fisherwoman Satyavati here, and that their son Ved Vyasa composed the Mahabharata in a riverside cave at the confluence, where his temple now stands.
20880: At Gandikota in Andhra Pradesh, the Penna has cut a dramatic gorge through the Erramala hills, narrowing to about 100 m, that is nicknamed the 'Grand Canyon of India'. A fort on its rim, first raised in 1123, was later held by the Golconda Sultanate and visited by the French traveller Tavernier.
21045: Kenduli on its banks, believed to be the birthplace of Jayadeva, the 12th-century poet of the Gita Govinda, hosts the Joydev Kenduli Mela every Poush Sankranti in mid-January, when Bauls gather in around 160 temporary hermitages to sing.
21067: Its flood of 20 July 1970 swept away Belakuchi, a roadside town near Pipalkoti, along with about 25 parked buses and trucks. Doing relief work there convinced Chandi Prasad Bhatt that the valley's forests had to be saved, three years before the Chipko movement began.
21221: The Asan Conservation Reserve, the wetland behind the Asan Barrage near where it joins the Yamuna west of Dehradun, became Uttarakhand's first Ramsar site in July 2020. Its winter visitors include bar-headed geese, ruddy shelducks and the rare Baer's pochard.
21587: Since 2009 Jaipur has drawn much of its drinking water from the Bisalpur dam on the Banas near Tonk, which also supplies Ajmer and Tonk. Its water has even been carried to Bhilwara by a 15-wagon water train from Nasirabad.
21629: The Jamwa Ramgarh dam on this river near Jaipur held the lake that hosted the rowing events of the 1982 Asian Games and was once the city's main water source. Mining and encroachment in its catchment have left it dry since the 2000s. Downstream, a channel feeds Bharatpur's Keoladeo bird sanctuary.
22045: The Gangotri temple on its bank was built not by a Garhwali king but by Amar Singh Thapa, a general of the Nepalese (Gorkha) army, and restored in the 19th century. Every winter, from Diwali to Akshaya Tritiya, the goddess's idol moves down to Mukhba village.
22405: In September 1893 a giant landslide blocked it, creating Gohna Tal. The British laid a telegraph line to the dam and posted watchmen, so when it burst in August 1894 the flood destroyed the town of Srinagar in Garhwal yet killed only about five people, who had refused to leave.
22590: About four out of five of the world's wild gharials live in the Chambal. Folk legend says the river was cursed by Draupadi, and that dread is credited with keeping people from settling on it, leaving it one of India's least polluted rivers.
22640: The wildlife sanctuary named after it, in the Vindhyan hills of eastern Uttar Pradesh, was chosen as a second home for Asiatic lions. Three lions from Gir, Raja, Rani and Jayshree, arrived in the late 1950s and grew to eleven by 1969, but by around 1970 all had vanished.
23260: Reni, the village near where the Rishi Ganga joins it, is where Gaura Devi and 27 other women faced down loggers on 25 March 1974, a defining moment of the Chipko movement. The government later banned tree-felling over more than 1,150 sq km of the area for ten years.
23685: IIT Roorkee began life in 1847 as a college to train the engineers and surveyors building the Ganges Canal, which draws Ganga water at Haridwar. When the canal opened in 1854, its main channel alone was about 560 km long, and near Roorkee it is carried for half a kilometre on an aqueduct.
24016: Delhi's next big source of drinking water is being built on it: the 148 m Renukaji dam, first surveyed in 1976 and finally begun in December 2021, will store about 498 million cubic metres, largely for the capital. Some 800 families in 35 villages are to be displaced.
24137: It rises at the Milam Glacier beside Milam village, home of Nain Singh Rawat, the explorer who walked about 1,580 miles across Tibet and was the first surveyor to fix the location of Lhasa. Once a busy Tibet-trade village of some 500 families, Milam has been almost deserted since the 1962 war.
24407: Alamgirpur, on its banks in Meerut district, is the easternmost known site of the Harappan (Indus Valley) civilisation. Partly excavated in 1958-59, it showed that the Harappan world reached into the Ganga-Yamuna doab, under 30 km from Delhi.
24470: Gartang Gali, a 136 m wooden walkway pinned to a cliff above its gorge in the Nelong valley, at about 11,000 feet, carried Tibetan traders bringing wool and salt. Said to have been built by Pathans from Peshawar, it was closed after the 1962 war and reopened to visitors in 2021.
24993: Gagron Fort near Jhalawar stands where the Ahu meets the Kali Sindh, with water on three sides and a moat on the fourth, making it a rare 'jal durg' or water fort. It is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.
26489: Chorabari Tal, a glacial lake in its headwaters just above Kedarnath, was renamed Gandhi Sarovar after some of Mahatma Gandhi's ashes were scattered in it. On 17 June 2013 its moraine wall burst, unleashing the Kedarnath flood, and the lake never refilled.
26630: The British built Port Canning on the Matla in the 1860s as a rival to Calcutta, despite meteorologist Henry Piddington's 1853 warning that a cyclone could swamp the site with a wall of seawater. An 1867 cyclone wrecked the town and the port closed in 1871-72; Canning is now a gateway to the Sundarbans.
27548: At Gaya it is usually a wide bed of sand: legend says Sita cursed it to run dry after it lied about her pind offering to Dasharatha. Since 2022 the 411-metre Gayaji Dam, India's longest rubber dam, holds water near the Vishnupad temple all year for pind daan.
27982: One of Rabindranath Tagore's last poems, written in May 1941, less than three months before his death, and collected in Shesh Lekha, opens with "Rupnaraner kule jege uthilam" (I woke on the banks of the Rupnarayan) and the realisation that this world is not a dream.
28010: It once filled the vast Najafgarh jheel in southwest Delhi, recorded in 1884 at over 220 sq km. Draining began in 1865, and channels dug after the 1964 and 1977 floods turned the river into today's Najafgarh Drain; the lake has shrunk to about 7 sq km.
28018: Pratapgarh's district town is formally 'Bela Pratapgarh', and the 'Bela' comes from the temple of Belha Devi (Bela Bhawani) on the Sai's bank. The town was simply called Bela until it became headquarters of the new Pratapgarh district in 1858.
28508: The Kshipra usually stops flowing a couple of months after the monsoon. Since 2014, Narmada water has been pumped up from the Omkareshwar reservoir and piped about 47 km to the Kshipra's source at Ujjaini village, keeping water flowing past Ujjain's Simhastha ghats. It was India's first river-linking project to rely on lifting water.
29033: Though counted as a tributary, it carries more water than the Yamuna when they meet below Kalsi. At that confluence stands a boulder carved with all 14 of Emperor Ashoka's major rock edicts around 250 BCE, the only full set in North India.
29220: Unlike its Himalayan neighbours, the Gomti has no glacier: it rises from a lake, Gomat Taal, in the Terai near Pilibhit, and is fed by rain and groundwater. At Jaunpur it is crossed by the Shahi Bridge, built on Akbar's orders and completed in 1568-69, which is still in use and inspired Kipling's poem 'Akbar's Bridge'.
29224: The Betwa is at the receiving end of India's first river-interlinking project. The Ken-Betwa link, whose foundation stone was laid on 25 December 2024, will carry surplus water from a new dam on the Ken into the Betwa basin to irrigate drought-prone Bundelkhand.
29239: Directly across the Yamuna from the Taj Mahal lies Mehtab Bagh, a Mughal 'moonlight garden' aligned exactly with the mausoleum. Excavations in the 1990s showed its supposed black marble was only discoloured white stone, and its octagonal pool throws back a dark reflection of the Taj, the likely origin of the 'Black Taj' legend.
29240: The sacred shaligram stones worshipped as Vishnu in homes across India are fossilised ammonites, sea creatures of the Jurassic period, gathered from the bed of the Kali Gandaki in Nepal, the Gandak's upper course. They are relics of the ancient Tethys sea that once lay where the Himalaya now stands.
29248: At the Uttarayani fair in Bageshwar on 14 January 1921, about 40,000 people gathered where it meets the Gomti, and village heads flung the registers of forced 'coolie begar' labour into the water. The British soon ended the practice; Gandhi called it a bloodless revolution.
29249: Its banks at Banda yield shajar, an agate in which seeping iron and manganese have drawn tree-like patterns ('shajar' means tree). The stones are traditionally found by the local Mallah community, and Banda's shajar stone craft received a GI tag in 2023.
29252: The Koilwar (Abdul Bari) Bridge over the Sone, opened in 1862, was India's longest river bridge until 1900 and is described as the oldest working railway bridge in the country, with trains running on top and a road underneath. It even appears in the 1982 film Gandhi.
29254: The Battle of Plassey in 1757, which gave the East India Company its hold over Bengal, was fought in a mango grove beside this river at Palashi, between Kolkata and Murshidabad. The river has since shifted and partly washed away the actual battlefield; a memorial obelisk marks the site.
29255: After a devastating flood in 1943, the Damodar became the testbed for independent India's first multipurpose river valley project. The Damodar Valley Corporation, set up in 1948, was modelled on America's Tennessee Valley Authority, and its plan was drawn up by one of that agency's senior engineers, W. L. Voorduin.
29279: Tradition holds that pind daan at Gaya is complete only after a first offering on the Punpun, where Rama is said to have made his first offering before going on to Gaya. Pilgrims at the Pitru Paksha Mela begin with rites here before moving to the Phalgu.
29296: Kolkata's port, about 203 km up this river from the sea, is India's only major river port and its oldest working one. The Farakka Barrage was built largely to push Ganga water into the Hooghly to flush silt from the harbour, though the diverted flow proved too weak to do the job fully.
29297: The Massanjore dam on it, commissioned in 1955, is also called the Canada Dam: it was funded through rupees raised from Canadian wheat aid and inaugurated by Canada's foreign minister, Lester B. Pearson. The river's name means "peacock's eye".
29298: At Taki, where the river is the India-Bangladesh border, Durga idols from both countries are taken out by boat on Vijaya Dashami and immersed at the mid-river boundary, with devotees on each side waving to each other.
29696: Called the Kali or Mahakali in the hills, where it forms India's border with Nepal, it becomes the Sharda in the plains. Building its barrage at Banbasa under a 1920 agreement needed land on the Nepali bank, so Nepal gave about 4,094 acres and received an equal area of forest from British India in exchange.
30271: India's deadliest rail accident happened here: on 6 June 1981 a crowded passenger train running between Mansi and Saharsa derailed on a bridge near Khagaria and plunged into the swollen Bagmati. The official toll was 235, but estimates run from 500 to over 800.
30273: "Burhi" means old: it flows in an old channel east of the present Gandak. Its meanders left behind Kanwar Lake (Kabartal) near Begusarai, Asia's largest freshwater oxbow lake, which in 2020 became Bihar's first Ramsar wetland.
30282: India's first national park, set up in 1936 as Hailey National Park, lies in the Patli Dun valley carved by the Ramganga. It was briefly renamed Ramganga National Park in the mid-1950s before taking Jim Corbett's name, and it was where Project Tiger was launched.
30294: Known as the Sarayu (Saryu) at Ayodhya, it is the Ganga's largest tributary by volume of water. Its ghats, including Ram ki Paidi, host the Ayodhya Deepotsav every Diwali; in 2025 over 26 lakh diyas lit along them set a Guinness World Record.
30314: Called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' for its floods, the Kosi shifted roughly 120 to 133 km westwards in the two centuries before it was embanked in the 1950s. In the 18th century it flowed near Purnia, which now lies far to the east of the river.
30323: Rising at Paglajhora Falls near Kurseong, it slips into Bangladesh near Tentulia for about 3 km, returns to India to flow past Siliguri and Malda, and finally re-enters Bangladesh to join the Ganga at Godagari.
40025: The Oshiwara neighbourhood, known for its antique and second-hand furniture market, takes its name from this river. The Western Railway station opened there in 2016 was planned as Oshiwara station but opened as Ram Mandir, after a nearby Ram temple first built in 1835.
